title: Why Old Coffins Had Doorbells #shorts

lines.text: In the eighteen hundreds, people were so scared of being buried alive, they started building coffins with doorbells.
Strings were tied to your hands and feet, and they ran up through the dirt to a little bell above your grave.
If you woke up underground, you just wiggled. Ding! Somebody would come dig you out.
One doctor was so sure about his design, he had himself buried alive to prove it.
He stayed down there for hours, and they even sent him a lunch of soup, sausages, and beer through a pipe.
Another inventor added a flag that popped up, and one man spent nine whole days inside his coffin.
Cemeteries hired night watchmen just to listen for bells.
And the bells did ring. A lot.
You see, after someone dies, the body swells up and shifts as it breaks down. So the strings would tug, and the bell would jingle.
It's like a smoke alarm that goes off every single time you make toast.
After all those inventions, bells, flags, and beer pipes, there's no record of a safety coffin ever saving a single person.
And no, that's not where saved by the bell comes from. That one's from boxing.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Safety coffin': Taberger's 1829 bell system with strings on the hands, head and feet and a cemetery night watchman; Dr Adolf Gutsmuth was buried alive several times to demonstrate his design and in 1822 ate soup, beer and sausages delivered through the pipe; Karnice-Karnicki's 1897 'Le Karnice' raised a flag and rang a bell, and in 1898 a man spent nine days in it; decay made bodies swell and shift, tugging the cords (false alarms); no documented case of anybody saved by a safety coffin; 'saved by the bell' comes from boxing
Australian Museum, 'Safety coffins': Taberger's 1829 design alerted a night watchman by a bell; bodies putrefy and bloat; no indication anyone was ever saved
Ripley's, 'Is the Phrase Saved by the Bell About Being Buried Alive?': the phrase is boxing slang for the end of a round
